concept: Burstable M10/M20 CPU-credit throttling and when to move to M30
summary: Source-anchored research for Burstable M10/M20 CPU-credit throttling and when to move to M30. Run status: COMPLETED.

facts.text: AWS describes burstable T instances as suitable for low-to-moderate CPU utilization and distinguishes Standard and Unlimited modes. Consequently, the generic statement that every AWS burstable instance must throttle immediately when earned credits run out is too broad; use Atlas-specific evidence when diagnosing Atlas. (low confidence)

Before attributing CPU pressure solely to tier size, inspect unoptimized queries and useful indexes. MongoDB recommends indexing as an immediate response and a larger cluster tier as a possible long-term response when the workload exceeds capacity. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-14)

Atlas Core uses Relative System CPU Utilization for M10/M20 auto-scaling: Normalized System CPU divided by baseline utilization, capped at 100%. The documented baseline range is typically 20%-50% and is not shown in Atlas metrics; with a 20% baseline, 15% normalized CPU equals 75% relative utilization. These example values do not establish a fixed baseline for every M10 or M20. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-30)

Atlas Core can scale M10/M20 operational nodes up when average relative CPU exceeds 75% for one hour, provided the next tier is within the configured maximum. An AWS-specific alternative requires relative CPU above 90% for 20 minutes plus non-normalized CPU steal above 30% for three minutes. Azure's corresponding provider-specific criterion uses softIRQ above 10% for three minutes. These are documented alternatives, not requirements that must all hold together. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-30)

A July 25, 2025 commenter on MongoDB's CPU-credit observability request reported M20 CPU Steal rising from 0% to 80% within minutes and severe service impact. This is a historical customer report, not a measured general depletion time or proof that every Atlas interface lacks credit telemetry. (low confidence)

A defensible M30 evaluation combines evidence of sustained CPU pressure or credit-exhaustion symptoms with query/index review, then compares the same workload on M30. MongoDB recommends indexes as an immediate CPU mitigation and a higher tier as a longer-term option; this does not establish that every slow query needs an upgrade. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-14)

Deyan Petrov's Azure account reports that moving to M30 did not resolve its disk-latency problem in March 2022; the November 2024 update instead attributes improved stability to Premium SSD v2. This historical counterexample scopes upgrade advice: M30 cannot be presumed to fix a bottleneck that was not CPU-credit throttling. (low confidence)

CPU credits accumulate below baseline utilization and are consumed above it. Azure B-series falls back to its baseline when credits run out; AWS Standard mode likewise returns gradually to baseline until credits accrue again. This explains why a short burst test cannot establish sustained CPU capacity. (medium confidence)

MongoDB recommends M30+ for production but explicitly supports M10/M20 for low-traffic production. Moving to M30 is a recommendation for workload suitability rather than a blanket requirement that every production deployment must satisfy. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-30)

A June 2021 DBA Stack Exchange question reproduced an Atlas alert stating that unsustainable CPU usage was being throttled and advising index checks and scale-up. The thread lacks enough workload and instance detail to establish a root cause, so it supports the existence of the reported symptom rather than an M30 sizing rule. (low confidence)

Decision inference: when an optimized workload repeatedly needs sustained CPU beyond M10/M20 burst capacity, evaluate M30 or higher instead of treating a move from M10 to M20 as eliminating bursting constraints. MongoDB identifies both smaller tiers as burstable and recommends upgrading when the current tier cannot support the workload. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-14)

Atlas warns that automatic scale-up needs time to prepare backing resources and may not occur in time for sudden bursts such as bulk inserts. Plan capacity increases before known spikes instead of assuming auto-scaling will prevent every resource shortage. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-30)

Atlas M10 and M20 use burstable infrastructure; cloud providers can cap CPU after burst periods and throttle sustained heavy workloads. A dedicated tier therefore does not guarantee sustained use of its full advertised vCPU capacity. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-30)

Atlas documents System: CPU (Steal) alerts as applicable to exhausted-credit AWS EC2 burstable M10/M20 instances. Do not generalize this alert to every provider: the Atlas Core auto-scaling criteria separately reference CPU steal for AWS and softIRQ for Azure. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-14)

In a February 24, 2025 Meteor forum post, an operator reported that upgrading a development workload to M30 resolved performance problems. The post reproduced MongoDB Support's diagnosis of CPU throttling on M10/M20 and recommendation to test on M30+. This is one operator report; the quoted support diagnosis is MongoDB-origin evidence, not another independent organisation. (low confidence)

AWS Unlimited mode qualifies the generalization that depleted credits always mean throttling: it can spend surplus credits and charge for sustained above-baseline usage. The cited Atlas documentation does not establish customer access to that mode, so EC2 Unlimited behavior is not evidence that Atlas M10/M20 avoids CPU throttling. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-30)
